q7.answer: The raw token is generated as 32 random bytes in the POST /password/forgot handler. Only its SHA-256 hash is stored in password_reset_tokens.token_hash. The raw token goes into the link https://<app-origin>/password/reset?token=<token>, which sits in the reset email job's payload. That job is inserted in the same transaction as the token, and the email worker sends the link through the mail provider. The job row is deleted once it is sent or dropped.

q8.answer: On GET /password/reset?token=T the server hashes T with SHA-256 and looks up the row with that token_hash. It then checks whether the row is ACTIVE: not consumed, not superseded, and expires_at greater than the database now(). If the row is active, the form is rendered with the token in a hidden field. Otherwise the 'link has expired' page is shown. POST repeats the same lookup and check.

q9.answer: There is no separate counter. The count is a SELECT count(*) over password_reset_tokens for that user_id where issued_at is greater than now() minus one hour. Old requests drop out of the window as now() moves forward. Rows are kept for 24 hours before the scheduled cleanup deletes them, which is longer than the one-hour window.

q10.answer: Only after the count check passes (fewer than 3 in the rolling hour), and in the same transaction as the new insert, the server runs an UPDATE that sets superseded_at = now() on every older row for that user where consumed_at and superseded_at are both NULL. A refused request does not supersede anything, so the existing active link stays usable.

q11.answer: In one transaction the server updates users.password_hash, sets consumed_at on the token row, deletes all of the user's sessions rows, and inserts the password_changed email job. Everything commits together or nothing changes. The confirmation email is queued inside that transaction, so it exists only if the reset commits. The worker sends it afterwards. The response then clears the session cookie and redirects with 303 to /login, without logging the user in.

q12.answer: The POST transaction runs SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the token row and then rechecks that the row is ACTIVE. The first submission commits and sets consumed_at. A concurrent second submission blocks on the row lock. Once it gets the lock, it sees the row is no longer active, rolls back, and shows the expired page. The length and breached-list checks run before the transaction and do not change state, so they do not affect this guarantee.
